misconception_description: Student believes that variable names containing vowels can only store string values, while consonant-only names can store any type.

solutions.generated_code:
program JumlahHarmonik
kamus
  n, ndx : integer
  value : string
  jumlah : real
algoritma
  input(n)
  jumlah <- 0
  for ndx <- 1 to n do
    value <- string(1 / ndx)
    jumlah <- jumlah + real(value)
  endfor
  output(jumlah)
endprogram

metadata.modification_notes: The student introduces an intermediate variable 'value' (which contains vowels 'a', 'u', 'e') to store the numeric result of 1/n. Following their misconception, they believe 'value' can only store strings, so they convert the numeric result to a string using str(). They then store the recursive result in 'rst' (no vowels), which they're comfortable storing as a number. When performing the addition, they convert 'value' back to float. The parameter 'n' has a vowel 'u', but the student accepts it as a parameter name (perhaps believing parameters are special). The code still produces correct results despite the unnecessary string conversions, making this a benign misconception that results in inefficient but functional code.
